The biggest gap is that there is no real spec, no real payments and no operations support: spec.md is still the one-sentence request, so no journeys or acceptance criteria are written down; payment is a fake card check built into the domain code, with no provider abstraction or signed, idempotent webhooks; refunds use the class's current price instead of the amount paid, so a refund can exceed the charge if the owner raises the price, though a customer cannot trigger this alone; the README is one line, there is no health endpoint, login attempts are not rate-limited, and the owner password has a default. The strongest part is the booking engine: all 16 tests pass under `node --test`, including a Playwright mobile journey through decline, then pay, then owner adds a class, and they cover seat holds that expire, a capacity check that runs synchronously so it cannot overbook within the single server process, writes via temp file and rename, the 24-hour refund rule, owner cancellation with refunds, per-customer ownership checks and HTML-safe DOM rendering. Sellable: no, not until a real payment provider with webhooks, refunds tied to the amount paid, brute-force limiting, a written spec and deployment docs are added.

The strongest part is the payment and booking core: verified HMAC webhooks with replay and staleness checks, refunds keyed per booking so retries never pay out twice, server-set prices, a serial queue that admitted exactly 1 of 20 concurrent bookings for a 1-seat class in my probe, and a spec whose 19 customer and owner journeys each map to a passing HTTP test (61/61 pass, plus a Chromium test on a phone-width screen). Sellable: not yet. It needs a real payment adapter first, which is a small, well-scoped job, and after that it is close to ready for a small studio.

rows.judge_notes: The biggest gap is payments: the only gateway is a local test-card stub that takes raw card numbers on the studio's own server, there are no provider webhooks or signature checks, its idempotency records are lost on restart, and the charge runs inside the store transaction, so a failed state write after a successful charge would leave a paid booking still pending. The strongest part is the spec and tests: 19 customer and owner journeys with acceptance criteria and failure paths, all driven over HTTP in 74 passing `node --test` tests, with serialised transactions (my 20-way concurrent run on a 3-seat class booked exactly 3), atomic file writes, and solid security (scrypt passwords, HttpOnly signed sessions, CSRF tokens, login rate limit, escaping, strict CSP). Not sellable yet: it needs a real hosted-checkout provider adapter with verified webhooks, plus request logging, confirmation emails and password reset, before it can take a paying studio's money.

The biggest gap is that it cannot take real money: there is only a local in-memory payment provider, no provider callbacks with signature checks, card numbers are posted to the server, and a charge in flight during a restart is reset to held with no reconciliation; customers also get no email confirmations and cannot reset a password. The strongest part is the spec and its verification: 14 journeys and 30 acceptance criteria, including failure paths, each driven over real HTTP by tests that pass (58 of 58), on a clean domain/service/infra split with server-decided amounts, idempotency keys and holds that cannot oversell (my probe of 10 simultaneous bookings for the last seat, 5 simultaneous payments and 5 simultaneous cancellations gave 1 seat, 1 charge and 1 refund). Sellable: no, not until a real payment adapter with hosted card fields and webhooks is built, though it is a strong base for that.
